chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Jameel, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

In the case of Al-Mubarat (divorce by disavowal), less than the dower is taken from her; and in the case of Al-Khul'a (divorce by redemption), he takes from her whatever he desires, or what they mutually agree upon from the dower or more. Al-Mubarat became such that less than the dower is taken from her, and Al-Khul'a is such that he takes whatever he desires, because the woman undergoing Al-Khul'a exceeds in speech and speaks what is not permissible for her.

key_terms.الصَّدَاق: The dower (Mahr) given to the wife.
key_terms.الْمُبَارِئَةُ: Al-Mubarat: A type of divorce where both parties disavow each other, typically involving a financial settlement less than the full dower.
key_terms.الْمُخْتَلِعَةُ: Al-Khul'a: A type of divorce initiated by the wife, involving a financial redemption paid to the husband.
key_terms.تَعْتَدِي فِي الْكَلَام: Exceeds in speech: A legal/technical phrase indicating the wife spoke words that justified the husband's claim to a larger portion of the dower.

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in dower deduction between Al-Mubarat and Al-Khul'a according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi distinguishes between Al-Mubarat, a mutual divorce where the husband retains less than the full dower, and Al-Khul'a, where the husband may retain any agreed-upon amount or more. The rationale provided—that the wife 'exceeded in speech' (i'taqat fi al-kalam)—reflects the Shia scholarly view that her verbal initiative or fault justifies the husband's financial claim, contrasting with the general principle of mutual consent in Mubarat.
